seal.statement: Ambient host async ancestry must never determine simulator execution-node attribution. Every simulate() establishes an explicit tracked generation root that overrides whatever async context invoked it, and the deterministic scheduler remains the only authority that introduces a node: the async hook may PROPAGATE node identity within one generation and may never ORIGINATE it from ambient host ancestry. A foreign ambient resource - the test runner's, a caller's promise, or one left from a previous generation - belongs to no active simulator generation and is charged to no simulator node; an active-generation production resource that requires a node and has none still fails closed with formation_execution_node_unbound. Three same-seed runs in one fresh process, with no warm-up run, produce one identical raw charging transcript and identical charged totals; the same seed charges identically under plain node and under node --test, through any ambient AsyncResource or promise ancestry, and across generations in one process.

text: The falsified assumption is confirmed and half repaired. Forensics first: the first attribution divergence between two same-seed runs in one process was at segment index 5, run 1 emitting unattributed@null where every later run emitted unattributed@node-0, and the first tracked resource of run 2 was a PROMISE whose trigger 227 was untracked - a resource left from run 1. Execution node came from an AsyncLocalStorage frame that ordinary Node propagation carried in from whoever called simulate(), so a fresh process gave the scenario root no frame and a later call inherited the previous generation's node-0. The repair gives every simulate() an explicit node-neutral generation root that overrides the caller's async context, tags every resource created inside that generation from the root onward - lineage tracking that begins before any scenario object exists, while the charging window keeps its own start and end - and refuses to open a simulator segment for a dispatch belonging to no active generation. Witness C, the ambient AsyncResource and promise-ancestry falsifier, and witness D, cross-generation isolation, both pass; witness E, the active-generation unbound refusal, still fails closed; the 429-entry metered scheduler oracle is byte-identical. Two production seams were needed: MessageRouter minted its routerId from the process entropy pool, so a deterministic run's transcript depended on how many UUIDs the process had minted (the pool refills on an async crypto request every 128 draws), and the lineage hook must carry no destroy callback because a tag that disappears on a garbage-collection schedule reintroduces exactly the nondeterminism being removed.

Witnesses A and B remain red for a residual with a different causal source, and the AVAILABLE discriminator names it exactly. Runs 2 and 3 are now identical to each other - 214,358 tagged dispatches and 106 correctly skipped foreign leftovers each - while run 1 has 214,671 tagged and 1 foreign, so the first simulation in a process still does 313 dispatches the later ones do not, 8 of them charged rather than unattributed. The owner's discriminator resolves what those are: the AVAILABLE planning read count still varies 49 to 51, and the FIRST differing invocation is not an attribution difference at all. Both runs read through the same call site, getPriorityRecoveryDecisionSnapshotForPartitionOperations from the priority-recovery follow-up decision path, but run 1 reads control_plane_publications-p1 first and run 2 reads replica_operations-p1 first. The coordinator's priority-partition iteration order differs between the first and later simulations in one process. That is production iteration order depending on process state, not ambient async ancestry, and it is a separate causal source that must be classified on its own before anything is resealed.

The drive-order premise is refuted by its own first discriminator, and the real owner is named instead. Membership is identical in every run and equal to resolvePriorityControlPlanePartitionIds(): six partitions, control_plane_publications-p1 first. The CALL sequence into getPriorityRecoveryDecisionSnapshotForPartitionOperations is canonical AND identical in every run - control_plane_publications, replica_operations, schema_operations, repeating - so O1, O2 and O3 are all refuted; nothing reconstructs an order from a Map, Set, cache row order or creation order. What differs is WHEN the reads of an earlier generation's calls land. Interleaving the CALL and READ logs shows run 2 opening with two READs that have no CALL in their own run, and the counts settle it: a single simulation in a fresh process performs 49 AVAILABLE reads while it runs and two more land AFTER simulate() has already returned, 49 becoming 51 on a 50 ms wait; four runs give 49, 51, 51, 51, each inheriting the previous generation's two late reads and leaking its own, with two more landing after the last run returns. So simulate() returns while production continuations it started are still owed, and they execute inside the next generation. Instant closure cannot see them because a pure promise chain queues no virtual event, and the owner-idle contracts cover only the gateway (awaitCurrentWorkIdle) and Raft (awaitCurrentProtocolIdle). The missing thing is the same shape as those two: a current-work completion contract for the rebalancer / workflow-owner follow-up decision path, consumed by the scenario's completion boundary. That is a scenario-completion owner, not an ordering owner.

Certification matrix complete and green in strict mode; the substrate is deterministic. Structural lane 488, A-F all six green with E still fail-closed. Same-process three runs byte-identical across every low-level artifact, not just the report: metered 391 entries hash a4c6ec504df54558, deterministic events 10,120 hash 8bd0a05c4da0ba84, raw attribution 277,623 segments hash ff530b9157cdc869, charge sequence hash 9a13ed89486e906c, report hash 4ff8340d202695d8, AVAILABLE reads 45. Three fresh processes produce exactly that same set, and node --test produces it too, with no runner-specific normalisation. Host-block 0, 50, 200 and 500 ms all identical - the probe burns a fixed iteration count rather than a timed loop, because reading the clock inside a node is what the guard now refuses and the probe must not be the rule-breaker. Observer matrix identical across no observer, observer enabled and observer with stack capture. Post-seal: zero production reads and zero attribution segments after return across six host checkpoints, and the next generation's report is identical. Invariants: zero unexpected formation_execution_node_unbound, joiner rebalancer 0,0,0,0 with node-0 the only rebalancer charge holder, worker_dispatch charged nowhere. Every contributing run carries ambientSeamMode strict, violations 0, substitutions 0, deterministicProofEligible true.

Measured datum from the F quest (formation-production-interaction-attribution-authority), recorded here because it belongs to this quest's subject rather than to F's.

Running the full production-composed seed chain UNDER the tap runner reaches ambient seams the deterministic owner guard counts: 1,306 strict violations, substitutions 0. The IDENTICAL code run as a script reports violations 0, substitutions 0, eligible true. Both arms are the same census over the same runSeedHandoffScenario at the same head; the only difference is the runner.

So the isolation defect is one-directional and loud rather than silent: it inflates violations under tap, it does not hide them. It also means a tap witness cannot gate the strict substrate for a full seed-chain scenario. F handled that by gating strict at its probe, which runs the census as a script, and by having the tap witness assert only what a runner cannot change - naming this quest as the owner of the gap rather than working around it quietly.

Not this quest: currentFormationExecutionContext (production-time-authority-closure) and the 9a39af51b captured-node change (the seed-host quest). Probe 0/6, exit 0. Red on revert: removing the generation root or the lineage filter fails A, C and D. Not pinned: removing the frame's generation filter or the routerId injection leaves 0/6, and B never fails under these mutations. Production is unchanged: no src code calls runOnSimulationGenerationRoot or runOnExecutionNode; an old-vs-new production-shaped attribution window gave a byte-identical snapshot; MessageRouterSetup never passes routerId. Focused files green (attribution 128/39/40, message-router 530/21). The 1bd9b3c70 residual "tap: 1,306 violations" is misattributed: plain node without logging init gives 1,306, tap with init 0, and every sample is the Date.now in LoggingService.shouldEmitMetricsMessage (logging-service-metrics-diagnostics.js:168) - a logging-clock owner, not runner isolation. The 429-oracle constraint cannot be re-checked, because that oracle was retired, and the new oracle JSON is read by no test. Seed 7 only. Says nothing about the formation defect.
